tagline.text: A cream-colored beach in Torrijos, Marinduque, facing Mount Malindig

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–500 (entrance, hut and kayak, per person)

children.text: Poctoy White Beach is the best-known beach in Barangay Poctoy, Torrijos, Marinduque. Locals call it white, but the sand is closer to cream, and you can swim, kayak and camp with Mount Malindig in view.

Poctoy White Beach is a beach in Barangay Poctoy, Torrijos, on the island of Marinduque. It is also called Torrijos White Beach, and travel sources describe it as the most prominent beach on the province's shores. Locals call it a "white" beach, but the sand is closer to cream. On clear days Mount Malindig, the highest peak in the province, can be seen in the distance. Several resorts and hut areas line the beach, and entrance and usage fees differ by area.
Torrijos is a town about
57 km

from the provincial capital Boac. It was established on May 25, 1880 by Real Order No. 469 and, in the 2024 census, had about 28,000 residents across 25 barangays. Wikipedia lists the town's attractions as Poctoy White Beach (Torrijos White Beach), the Battle of Pulang Lupa Monument in Bolo, Ka Amon Cave in Bonliw, Freedom Park in the town center, Sibuyao Farms, Bonliw Loom Weaving and Tabag Cliff and River in Malibago. The trip is long just for the beach, so it works well to combine it with these places for a full day. Torrijos covers about
179 km²

, from the coast up to mountains over 1,000 meters high, and became a parish of Santa Cruz in 1884. In 1900 Philippine revolutionary forces are said to have dealt the Americans a major setback at the Battle of Pulang Lupa, so some travelers add a bit of history to the beach. During World War II the Japanese occupied the town in 1942 and the Battle of Marinduque was fought in and around Torrijos in 1945.

According to travel sources, Poctoy is a place of simple pleasures. You swim in shallow clear water, rest in the shade of a hut, take photos with Mount Malindig in the background, and play beach volleyball or kayak. Stalls on the beach sell halo-halo and sago't gulaman, and vendors walk around selling twisted fried snacks (pilipit) and vegetable spring rolls (lumpiang gulay). You may bring your own food but should eat it only inside the pavilion or hut you paid for, and food and drinks are reportedly not allowed on the shore or in the water.

The beach is known to be very crowded during Holy Week and on weekends when local travelers arrive. If you want quiet, choose a weekday morning, and during Holy Week, when the Moriones Festival takes place, expect crowds and book ahead. Because the trip is long and public transport connections are limited, leave slack in your schedule and check return transport when starting from Boac or Gasan. Poctoy is not a resort near Manila with facilities but a modest local beach. Rather than expecting big hotels or shopping, think of it as a place to enjoy sand and hut shade among local families, and you will be less disappointed. Visitors are encouraged to take their own trash away to reduce litter on the beach.
Despite the name "white sand," the sand is cream-colored. You can swim in shallow, clear water, and sources advise anyone who is not a strong swimmer to avoid swimming far out.
On clear days Mount Malindig, Marinduque's highest peak, appears beyond the beach. Early morning and sunset are good times for photos.

There are stalls with cool treats such as halo-halo and sago't gulaman, and vendors selling twisted fried pilipit and vegetable spring rolls. You need cash.
The Battle of Pulang Lupa Monument (September 13, 1900), Ka Amon Cave, Bonliw Loom Weaving, and Tabag Cliff and River are listed on Wikipedia as places worth combining with the beach.

If you arrange a rental car or a car with a driver, it is easier to combine a circuit of Marinduque with Torrijos' other sights besides the beach. Public transport timetables may not fit and make a day trip tight, so check your return ride first and then decide how long to spend at the beach.

Marinduque has a tropical climate without a sharply defined dry season, but February to May generally has clear seas that are good for swimming. During Holy Week and on weekends the beach gets crowded with local travelers.
For a quiet beach, weekday mornings are best. From June to November rain is frequent and waves can limit swimming, and getting around is less convenient.
Before 10 AM and after 4 PM the sun is gentler and there are fewer people. Around noon there is little shade and the heat is intense, so rest in a hut or pavilion and drink plenty of water.

Torrijos has resorts and hut areas near the beach, and sources list Beach Club Cagpo and Villa Briones as lodging. Check rates and condition. You can stay in Boac or Gasan and come for the day, but the trip is long, so staying overnight near the beach is more relaxed.

Food is basically halo-halo and sago't gulaman from beach stalls and snacks from vendors. There are not many restaurants, so prepare lunch yourself or buy it in advance in Torrijos town. You are told to eat only inside the hut or pavilion you paid for.
You need cash. ATMs are said to be rare and cards are rarely accepted. Bring enough cash, with your return transport in mind.

Marinduque is a distant island that takes nearly a day from Manila, so keep that in mind first. Rather than coming only for the beach, a trip of three or more nights that combines the old church in Boac, island hopping to the Tres Reyes Islands and the Moriones Festival in Holy Week gives more for the travel effort.
A weekday morning is much quieter.
Bring plenty of cash. ATMs and card payments are rare.
Tents can be pitched only in the designated area and only at night.
Eat only inside your hut or pavilion and do not take food to the shore or into the water.
Use sunscreen free of ingredients harmful to coral.
Bring a dry bag, a reusable water bottle and a shopping bag so you leave no trash.
Unless you are a strong swimmer, do not go far from shore.
Check the last return transport time first.
Entrance and hut fees differ by business, so compare two or three places rather than deciding after seeing one.
Swimming far from shore is dangerous, so avoid it unless you are experienced, and secure transport before dark.
During Holy Week and on weekends the beach is very crowded and lodging can sell out.
ATMs are rare, so running short of cash can be a problem.
The last jeepney leaves early, so your return transport can end.
Fees and rules differ by area, so check prices and what is allowed before entering.
Some areas allow food and drinks only inside huts, so follow the rules.
The island province with Poctoy Beach, known for the Moriones Festival and the old church in Boac. Torrijos is about
57 km
from Boac.
The provincial capital, with an old church, museum and town scenery. It combines well into a day before or after the beach.
Wikipedia lists a monument in Bolo, Torrijos, commemorating the Battle of Pulang Lupa, fought between Philippine revolutionary forces and American troops on September 13, 1900.
Three islands, Gaspar, Melchor and Baltazar, off Gasan. You can visit them by island hopping and continue your trip on the same island as Torrijos.
